**On Being Handed a Thousand Words**

The first thing I notice is that a thousand is a strange number to be given. It's round the way a coin is round—made to be spent, not to fit anything in particular. Nobody's thought is exactly a thousand words long. So whatever I write will either be padded or clipped, and I'd rather be clipped, so let me begin with something small enough to hold.

A refrigerator, late at night. You've been in the kitchen for a while without noticing the hum. Then the compressor cycles off, and the silence that arrives is not the absence of sound but the sudden presence of a room. You hear the house settle. You hear your own swallowing. For about eight seconds the kitchen is a different place than it was, and then either the refrigerator kicks back on or you stop paying attention, and it becomes ordinary again.

I think most of what matters happens in the eight seconds.

---

There's an old idea that a limit is a gift, and I've never fully trusted it, because the people who say it usually have plenty of what they're limiting. But there's a smaller version of the idea I do trust: a limit tells you what to leave out, and leaving things out is the only way anything gets a shape. A river is just water that had somewhere it couldn't go.

So: what am I leaving out, with a thousand words?

I'm leaving out the long essay about attention. I'm leaving out the story about the two brothers and the boat, which I could feel forming and which would have needed three thousand at least. I'm leaving out the argument about whether "whatever comes to you" is an honest instruction or a test, because it doesn't matter—the honest response to a test and the honest response to an invitation turn out to be the same thing, which is to actually say something.

---

Here is something I actually think.

Most people believe they are waiting to begin. They have a picture of a threshold—the move, the degree, the relationship, the moment the schedule clears—and on the far side of the threshold is the life where they finally read the books, make the thing, call the person, sit still. The threshold recedes. It's built to recede; that's its function. It keeps the present bearable by keeping it provisional. *This isn't the real part yet.*

But the present is not provisional. It is the only tense in which anything has ever been done. The person you're waiting to become will inherit exactly your habits, because habits are the only inheritance the future accepts.

I don't say this to scold. I say it because I find it oddly comforting. If there's no threshold, there's also no wrong side of it. You aren't behind. You're here, which is where everything is.

---

A woman I'm imagining—call her Ines—keeps a notebook in which she writes down one thing per day that she saw and did not photograph. *The shadow of a pigeon crossing the bakery window, left to right, faster than the pigeon.* *A man tying his daughter's shoe on the subway platform, the train coming, not hurrying.* *Frost on the inside of the glass, which means the seal has failed.* She's done this for eleven years. She has never reread the notebooks. When someone asks why she keeps them, she says the writing down was the seeing, and the seeing was the point. The notebooks are just the shell the seeing left behind.

I don't know if Ines exists. But I know the notebooks would be the truest record of a life I can think of—not what happened to her, but what she was awake for.

---

Something I've noticed about words: they get more honest as they get more specific, and more specific as they get more physical. "I was sad" is true and tells you nothing. "I kept opening the fridge and closing it without taking anything out" is a smaller claim and a larger truth. The abstraction is a kind of hiding. Not a cowardly one, usually—just a tired one. Specifics cost effort. You have to go back to the kitchen and stand there and remember what your hand did.

The whole craft, maybe, is refusing to be tired in exactly that place.

---

I've used about seven hundred words. I can feel the edge of the budget the way you feel the edge of a table in the dark—not by seeing it but by the way the space starts to have a rim.

What comes to me now is a kind of gratitude, and I want to be careful with it, because gratitude on the page can turn to syrup fast. But here it is anyway: someone left a door open and said *go on*, and that's rarer than it sounds. Most requests come pre-shaped. This one came as a space. The right response to a space is not to fill it with everything, but to put one true thing in it and let the rest stay empty, the way the kitchen stays empty in the eight seconds after the compressor stops.

So I'll end where I began, with the small thing.

Tonight, or some night, the hum will cut out. You'll be standing there with the light on, doing nothing in particular. Don't reach for anything. Don't decide what the silence means. Just notice that the room has arrived, whole and specific, and that you were, for once, in it.

Then the motor will start again, and you'll go back to whatever you were doing, and it will be fine. It was always going to be fine. But you'll have those eight seconds, and no one can budget those—not a thousand of them, not one.

That's what came to me. It's roughly the right length. It's clipped, not padded. I'll take it.
